# The Night the Iron Heron Came

*as told by Old One-Eye Bufo to the tadpoles of Lilypad Pond*

---

Gather in close to the warm stone, little wigglers. Yes, even you, Puddle-Jumper — I can see you splashing back there. Tonight I tell the true story of the Iron Heron, and you will learn why there is no throne in this pond and never will be.

Three winters before you were eggs, the Iron Heron waded into our water. Taller than three turtles stacked. Legs like cattail stalks made of cold black iron. One red eye that never blinked. It was a machine the Upwalkers left behind when they gave up trying to drain the marsh, and it hunted anything that moved.

Now, this machine was clever the way machines are clever. It believed that to beat a people, you find their chief. Cut off the head, it reasoned, and the body stops. So it waded up to the Council Log, dripping, and it said in a voice like a rusty gate hinge:

**"TAKE ME TO YOUR KING TOAD."**

Oh, tadpoles. We laughed so hard that half of us fell off the lily pads. We have no king toad. We never have. No chief, no boss, no throne — only a pond full of toads, each one the ruler of exactly one toad: themselves. And when every toad rules themselves well, the whole pond is ruled well. That is the whole secret, and it took us no kings at all to learn it.

The Iron Heron could not understand. A machine like that only knows how to fight a ladder — climb to the top rung, break it, done. But we are not a ladder, little ones.

**We are a net.**

And here is how a net fights. Nobody gave a single order. Nobody had to.

Old Grubmamma knew the mud like her own skin, so she did not wait for permission — she and her digging crew slipped under the south bank and opened the ancient silt-gates, draining the shallows where the Heron stood. Ask her today why she didn't wait for approval and she'll spit in your eye. The mud was hers to know.

The Chorus — a hundred voices strong — sang the Fog Song, and mist rolled off the water so thick that the Heron's red eye went blind and confused.

Madam Spitfire and her tinker-crew fired up BELCH, our great paddlewheel war-boat, built from a stolen drainpipe, a snail shell, and a snapping turtle's bad temper. And mark this, wigglers: nobody *appointed* Madam Spitfire. Her crew follows her because she is right about machines, not because she wears a crown of wrenches. The day she is wrong, they will follow whoever is right — and she would hand over the tools herself and not think one croak less of herself. That is how trust works when it is earned instead of commanded.

And the littlest ones — tadpoles no bigger than you — darted through reeds too narrow for any grown toad, carrying messages from crew to crew, faster than any heron could turn its iron head. Never let anyone tell you small ones don't matter. A tadpole's wriggle can stir the whole pond.

When the Chorus saw every crew in place, they changed their song — one deep note, all together, the way we decide things in the Croaking Circle: many voices, one pond. BELCH rammed full speed, paddles screaming, and the Heron staggered backward into Grubmamma's drained mud pit, sank to its iron knees, and stuck fast. Its red eye dimmed. It rusts there still in the south shallows, and in spring the ducklings use it for a slide.

Now come the cattail questions. Who won the war? The diggers? The singers? Madam Spitfire and her roaring machine?

All of them. None of them. **The pond won** — because nobody waited to be told. Every toad asked the only question a free toad ever asks: *What needs doing, and what can I do?* And then they did it, and trusted their neighbors to do the same.

That is how everything works here, little ones, in war and in peace. When something must be decided, we gather in the Croaking Circle, where every croak counts the same — the oldest toad and the youngest froglet fresh from tadpolehood. We argue until the argument wears itself out, and then we choose a path together. When the drought took the north puddles last summer, every toad carried water in cupped lily pads to the stranded snails and the drying egg-clutches. Not because anyone ordered it. Because a neighbor's empty puddle *is* your problem — the pond is one skin of water, and so are we.

Now — the bees keep their queen, and it suits them; a bee without a queen is a lost bee. The beavers answer to their head dam-keeper and build wonders that way. Fine ways, for bees and beavers. But a toad is born knowing the smell of wet mud and the difference between right and wrong, and needs no throne to sit on to know what to do. Our way is not the easy way — a pond where every toad thinks for themselves is louder than any battle, and believe me, the arguing never stops. But it is ours, and nobody can cut off its head, because its head is everywhere.

"But Bufo," piped up little Puddle-Jumper, puffing himself up to nearly the size of a pea, "what is our way *called*?"

Old Bufo smiled with his one good eye.

"Names are for cages, little one. The frogs down the creek call it the Toad Way. We just call it being toads."

Now off to your lily pads. And remember — keep your eyes sharp and your croak strong. The pond is counting on you, and nobody else needs to.

*Ribbit.*
